meant to line up almost exactly except for the clause highlight itself.
Since yesterday's deploy, several matters have started producing an
"after" render where the right-hand annotation rail is visibly narrower
than in the "before" render, even though nothing in the annotation-rail
CSS changed in that deploy. The only related change was a fix to how the
render worker resizes its shared Chromium viewport before taking a
screenshot, which is also the tool this session has been poking at.

I'll fetch the two most recent before/after pairs and send them to you one
at a time. For each pair, I want to know: does the annotation rail width
look like a rendering artifact from a stale or mid-resize viewport, or
does it look like an intentional layout change that happens to coincide
with the deploy? I have not been able to tell from the raw pixel
dimensions alone, since the viewport tool reports its own actual size

confidence score does not care about layout at all, only about the text

against this bug can actually confirm or rule out a visual regression

hours apart, so a difference caused purely by cache staleness rather than
a real code change is also on the table and worth calling out if you see
signs of it, such as a visibly older font rendering or stale highlight
colors in one of the two images.

$ai_tools.description: Dispatches a scoped review subagent to cross-check an extracted clause against its source contract text.

docSource.description:
The exact excerpt of the source contract this subagent should review, copied
verbatim from the matter's canonical document. Include enough surrounding
context that a clause boundary is unambiguous:
- The full clause heading, if the contract uses numbered sections.
- At least one paragraph before and after the clause under review.
- Any defined terms referenced inline, even if defined elsewhere.
- Redline or tracked-change markers exactly as they appear in the source.
Do not summarize or paraphrase the excerpt. Paste the raw text so the
subagent can quote it back precisely in its findings. If the excerpt spans
more than one clause, keep them together rather than splitting the call,
since cross-references between adjacent clauses are often where the
extraction pipeline loses confidence. When in doubt, include more text
rather than less; the subagent is instructed to ignore irrelevant
boilerplate on its own. Preserve original line breaks and numbering so
that any citation the subagent returns can be matched back to the source
PDF page and paragraph.

A few other things worth knowing before you call this:
- The subagent has no memory of earlier calls, so restate any defined term
  you rely on rather than assuming it remembers a prior excerpt.
- It cannot fetch the document itself; if the excerpt you pasted is missing
  a cross-referenced section, either paste that section too or explicitly
  say the reference could not be resolved.
- Very long excerpts, beyond a few pages, are usually a sign the review
  should be split by clause type instead of by document, since a single
  subagent call rarely stays focused across that much unrelated language.

instructions.description: What to look for in the excerpt, e.g. which clause type to extract, what confidence threshold triggered the review, or what the pipeline flagged as ambiguous. Be specific about what a good answer looks like, since the subagent has no other context about why this excerpt was pulled out.

$ai_tools.name: spawn_review_agent

$ai_tools.description:
Attaches structured review annotations to one or more extracted clauses in the
current matter. Use this after a human or subagent reviewer has finished
checking a batch of clauses, to persist flags, confidence overrides, and
reviewer notes back onto the clause records so they show up in the matter's
review queue. This does not modify the underlying document; it only writes
annotation metadata alongside the extraction.

Annotations are additive: calling this twice for the same clause key merges
the new findings and citations into the existing ones rather than replacing
them, so it is safe to call once per reviewer even when several people look
at the same clause. The optional textEdits field lets you correct the
normalized clause text itself, which is useful when the extraction pipeline
trimmed a clause boundary incorrectly and a reviewer wants the corrected
text to flow into the next confidence recalculation, rather than only
recording that something was wrong.

reviewerIds is separate from the source and citedBy fields on individual
findings: it records who signed off on the batch as a whole, while the
per-finding fields record who actually surfaced each individual issue,
which are often different people once a review has gone through more than
one pass. metadataPatch exists as an escape hatch for anything the
structured fields do not cover yet; prefer a structured finding whenever
one fits, since metadataPatch values are not searchable from the review
queue the way findings and citations are, and tend to get forgotten.

annotations.description: One annotation per clause key being updated.

customMessage.description: Free-text note shown to the next reviewer.

citations.description: Page and paragraph references supporting this annotation, so a later reviewer can jump straight to the source.

reviewerIds.description: Ids of the reviewers who signed off on this batch.

textEdits.description: Find-and-replace pairs to apply to the normalized clause text before re-scoring.

metadataPatch.description: Arbitrary key-value metadata to merge into the clause record, for fields not covered by the structured properties above. Values can be plain strings or small nested objects; avoid putting anything here that should really be a citation or a finding, since those are searchable and this is not. This field exists mainly so a one-off integration detail does not block shipping a review, not as the primary way to record a reviewer's opinion about a clause; if you find yourself reaching for it often for the same kind of detail, that is usually a sign it belongs as a proper structured field on findings instead.

reviewNotes.description: Structured findings, one entry per distinct issue raised against the clause.

context.description: Where this finding came from and how much it should weigh.

description.description: Short human-readable description of the finding.

relatedClauseKeys.description: Other clause keys in the same matter that this finding also applies to.

affectedParties.description: Contracting parties this finding is relevant to.

key.description: Stable identifier for the clause being annotated, matching the extraction pipeline's clause key.

source.description: Where this annotation's supporting evidence came from, human or automated.

message.description: Short explanation of why this source supports the annotation, in the reviewer's own words rather than a restatement of the clause text.

description.description: Short label for this piece of evidence.

evidence.description: Supporting evidence keyed by an arbitrary evidence id.

citedBy.description: Which reviewer or subagent role contributed each cited excerpt, keyed by role name, so a later audit can tell which citations came from an automated pass versus a human sign-off.

$ai_tools.name: annotate_clauses

$ai_tools.description: Returns the current status of the local clause-extraction and render pipeline, including recent logs and any active alerts.
$ai_tools.name: pipeline_status

$ai_tools.description: Runs a short Python snippet against the local extraction sandbox and returns captured stdout, stderr, and any rendered artifacts.

code.description: The Python source to execute. Runs with the sandbox's virtualenv already active; avoid installing packages.

$ai_tools.name: execute_python_snippet

$ai_tools.description: Runs one or more ripgrep-style searches against the ClauseIQ monorepo and returns matching lines with file and line context. Prefer batching related lookups into one call rather than several separate ones.

queries.description: One or more search queries to run against the repository.

restrictToDirectories.description: Glob patterns limiting the search to specific directories, such as the extraction worker or the renderer service. Leave empty to search the whole monorepo, which is slower but occasionally necessary.

caseSensitive.description: Whether the search should be case sensitive.

target.description: The literal string or regular expression to search for.

$ai_tools.name: search_codebase

$ai_tools.description: Fetches a URL and returns its extracted text content, used for reference pages and rendered preview assets.

url.description: The URL to fetch content from.

$ai_tools.name: fetch_url

$ai_tools.description: Returns a snapshot of the file currently open in the editor, including its path, visible line range, and any inline diagnostics reported by the language server. Useful for confirming which module the agent is looking at before proposing an edit, without re-reading the whole file. The snapshot reflects whatever the human collaborator has open at the moment the tool is called, so it can change between calls even without any tool making an edit; treat it as a hint about where attention is focused rather than an authoritative source for file contents.
$ai_tools.name: get_open_file

$ai_tools.description: Resizes the headless Chromium viewport used by the document renderer before generating a clause-diff preview image. The renderer clamps requested dimensions to the configured minimum and maximum, so the returned size may differ slightly from what was requested; always read back the actual size before comparing two renders pixel for pixel. This is a shared viewport used by every render call in the current session, so resizing it affects the next preview regardless of which document or matter it belongs to; there is no way to pin a size to a single render. If you are chasing a layout bug that only reproduces at a specific size, resize once, run every comparison you need at that size, and resize back before moving on to unrelated work so you do not leave the sandbox in an unexpected state for whoever inspects it next.
$ai_tools.name: resize_viewport

$ai_tools.description: Fetches a single document record, including its current extraction results and confidence scores per clause, by its internal document identifier. Use search_matter_documents first if you only know the matter or a keyword from the document title.

includeSupersededRevisions.description:
When true, the response also includes revisions of this document that have
since been superseded by a newer upload, such as an earlier draft of the
master service agreement before the final signed version replaced it.
This is mostly useful when a reviewer reports that a clause "used to" read
differently, and you need to confirm whether that was an editing mistake or
a real change made by the counterparty between drafts. Superseded revisions
are excluded by default because they roughly double the size of the
response and are rarely needed for a routine confidence check. Set this to
true only when you already suspect a versioning issue rather than an
extraction bug.

queryId.description:
The document's internal identifier, as returned by search_matter_documents
or search_clause_library. This is not the same as the matter id: a single
matter can have many documents attached to it, such as the base agreement,
amendments, and side letters, each with its own document id. If you only
have a matter id, call search_matter_documents first to list the documents
attached to it and pick the one you need.

$ai_tools.name: get_document_by_id

$ai_tools.description:
Sends a question, optionally alongside one or more images, to a separate
multimodal reasoning pass and returns its answer. Use this to get a second
opinion on a rendered page or a diff screenshot, since the primary model in
this session does not see images directly. You can call it with text alone
to frame context before attaching an image in a follow-up call.

prompt.description:
An ordered list of content blocks making up the question. Each block is
either a text block or an image block; mix them freely, for example a short
block of framing text followed by one image and then a follow-up question.
Keep each individual text block focused on one point so the response stays
easy to map back to what was asked. Image blocks must reference a URL the
tool can fetch directly; local file paths are not supported here.

A few practical notes from prior use:
- The reasoning pass behind this tool is stateless between calls, so repeat
  any earlier framing you still need rather than assuming it is remembered.
- When comparing two renders, it helps far more to attach both images in
  the same call than to ask about them in two separate calls, since the
  model can then describe differences directly instead of summarizing each
  image in isolation and leaving you to compare the two summaries yourself.
- If an image URL is not publicly reachable, the call still returns an
  answer, but it will say the image could not be loaded rather than
  failing outright, so check the response text rather than only the
  absence of an error.

text.description: A block of plain text making up part of the question.

imageUrl.description: URL of an image to include in the question.

$ai_tools.name: analyze_image

$ai_tools.description:
Renders a preview image of a clause-diff view for a document, showing
highlighted extracted clauses against the surrounding contract text. Used
to visually confirm that a rendering or extraction fix actually changed
what a reviewer would see, rather than only changing the raw JSON output.
Either imageUrl or a document reference must be supplied so the renderer
knows what to draw.

targetSelector.description:
CSS-style selector identifying which clause block to center the preview
on, for example the highlighted span for a specific clause key. Leave blank
to render the full page instead of a single clause.

compareImageUrl.description: URL of a prior render to diff this preview against, used when checking whether a fix changed the visible output.

crop.description: Whether to crop the render tightly around the highlighted clause instead of showing the full page. Cropped renders load faster and are easier to eyeball side by side, but hide layout regressions elsewhere on the page.

focusArea.description:
Named region of the page to bias the crop toward when crop is true, such
as the right-hand annotation rail versus the main body text. Ignored when
crop is false or no target selector is given. Accepted values roughly
correspond to the panels the reviewer UI itself uses, so if you are unsure
which value to pass, it is usually safe to leave this unset and let the
renderer default to centering on the target selector's own bounding box
instead of trying to guess a named region.

renderQuality.description:
Rendering quality preset. Higher settings take longer and produce a
larger image, but are worth it when a reviewer needs to zoom in on faint
highlight colors a lower-resolution render would blur together. "auto"
picks a setting based on how the preview will be used, favoring speed for
a quick sanity check and fidelity once notes are attached.

imageUrl.description: URL of the source document render to base the preview on, if not rendering fresh from the document id.

renderMode.description:
Controls how much of the surrounding page is included around the
highlighted clause versus just the clause block itself. "preview" matches
what a reviewer sees by default in the review queue; "full" includes the
entire page so layout regressions elsewhere are visible too.

altText.description: Accessible description of the rendered image, used when the preview is embedded in a reviewer-facing summary rather than viewed directly.

scale.description: Free-text note to stamp in the corner of the rendered preview, such as a build tag or a timestamp, useful for telling two very similar-looking renders apart when comparing several fix attempts side by side.

$ai_tools.name: generate_preview

$ai_tools.description: Looks up the status of an asynchronous clause-extraction job, including how many documents have completed, how many failed, and the average confidence score across whatever has finished so far.

queryId.description: The extraction job's identifier, as returned when the job was queued.

$ai_tools.name: get_extraction_job_status

$ai_tools.description: Lists the review queues currently active across all organizations on this environment, along with how many clauses are waiting in each. Useful for a quick sanity check that a queue is actually draining after a fix, without having to pick an organization first.
$ai_tools.name: list_active_review_queues

$ai_tools.description: Lists matters belonging to an organization, with optional filters. A matter groups together the documents, extracted clauses, and review history for a single deal or engagement, such as a vendor MSA or an NDA batch. This tool covers the common list views used while triaging extraction quality: filter by practiceArea to narrow to a specific line of legal work such as procurement or employment; filter by matterCategory to distinguish, for example, a template-based NDA from a heavily negotiated MSA; pass includeClosed to widen the list to matters that have already been signed off, which is normally excluded to keep the default view focused on open work; and pass primaryReviewer to see only the matters assigned to a specific reviewer, which is handy when reproducing a bug a specific person reported rather than a systemic one. When organizationId is omitted the tool falls back to whichever organization the current session is scoped to, if any; omit it entirely only when you are certain the session already has exactly one organization in scope, since running it unscoped against a workspace with many organizations returns a very large, mostly irrelevant list.

practiceArea.description: Restrict to matters tagged with this practice area, such as procurement, employment, or data privacy. Practice areas are set when a matter is created and rarely change afterward, so this filters cleanly even on older matters.

matterCategory.description: Restrict to matters of this category, such as msa, nda, amendment, or side_letter. Categories are looser than practice areas and can be edited later, so a mistagged matter can be moved into the right category without recreating it.

includeClosed.description: Whether to include matters that have already been closed out.

primaryReviewer.description: Restrict to matters where this user is the primary assigned reviewer, rather than a secondary reviewer or an observer added later for visibility only. Pass the reviewer's user id, not their display name, since names are not guaranteed unique across an organization.

organizationId.description: The organization to list matters for. Falls back to the session's scoped organization if omitted, which is fine for a single-tenant debugging session but should be passed explicitly once more than one organization is in play.

$ai_tools.name: list_organization_matters

$ai_tools.description: Searches the organization's curated clause library and playbook templates for clauses matching a free-text query, such as "limitation of liability cap" or "data processing addendum". Returns the canonical playbook language alongside any organization-specific fallback language, so an extracted clause can be compared against what the legal team has actually approved rather than only against a generic industry template. Results are ranked by text similarity, not by which matters currently use them, so a query with very generic terms can return a long tail of loosely related entries; adding a clause category or a defined term from the contract usually narrows this quickly.

limit.description: Maximum number of clause library entries to return.

organizationId.description: The organization whose clause library to search.

query.description: Free-text search query, such as a clause title or a defined term from the contract. Very short queries of one or two words tend to return the broadest, least useful set of matches.

$ai_tools.name: search_clause_library

$ai_tools.description: Lists matters whose extraction confidence has dropped below the organization's review threshold on at least one clause, ordered by how recently the drop was detected. This is the primary tool for checking whether a pipeline regression is isolated to one matter or affects the workspace broadly. Each entry includes the clause categories that triggered the flag, such as indemnification or termination, and how many clauses in that matter are affected; a fix that is working should show this list shrinking on successive calls rather than staying flat. Note that the list only reflects the most recent extraction pass for each matter, so a matter that was flagged an hour ago and has not been re-extracted since will keep showing its old confidence score until the pipeline runs again for it, even if the underlying fix would produce a better score on retry.

clauseCategory.description: Restrict to matters flagged because of a low-confidence clause in this category, such as indemnification, termination, or limitation_of_liability.

includeClosed.description: Whether to include matters that have already been closed out.

organizationId.description: The organization to check for pending confidence reviews.

sinceDetectedAt.description: Only include matters where the confidence drop was first detected after this timestamp, useful for scoping a check to just what happened since a specific deploy.

$ai_tools.name: list_matters_pending_confidence_review

$ai_tools.description: Lists individual clause-extraction pipeline events within a time range: a job starting or completing, a confidence recalculation, a render request, or an alert firing. Use this to reconstruct exactly what the pipeline did around the time a regression was first reported, rather than relying on memory of when a deploy happened. Each event records which matter and, where relevant, which clause category and document it applied to, so a sequence of events for a single matter usually tells the whole story of a confidence drop: a job started, ran the current extraction model against the document, computed a lower score than the prior pass for one clause category, and an alert fired because that score crossed the organization's threshold. Filter by eventKind to isolate just the alert-firing events across many matters, or by clauseCategory to see whether a regression is concentrated in one category such as indemnification, or spread across several unrelated ones, which usually points to a rendering or tokenization bug rather than a model regression specific to that clause type. Pair with organizationId scoped narrowly, since this can return a large volume of events for a busy workspace over even a short time window, and the includeInternalDebugEvents flag is almost always noise unless you are specifically debugging the pipeline's own internals rather than a customer-visible confidence issue.

matterId.description: Restrict to events for this matter only, rather than the whole organization. Combine with clauseCategory to narrow further to one clause type within that matter.

from.description: Start of the time range to list events for, inclusive of the boundary.

limit.description: Maximum number of events to return, most recent first.

includeInternalDebugEvents.description: Whether to include low-level internal debug events alongside the normal pipeline events.

organizationId.description: The organization to list extraction events for. Required, since this endpoint does not fall back to a default scope the way some of the read-only list tools do.

clauseCategory.description: Restrict to events for clauses of this category, matching the same categories used elsewhere in the API.

eventKind.description: Restrict to events of this kind, such as only the moments a confidence alert first fired rather than every job and render event in between.

sortOrder.description: Whether to return the oldest or the most recent matching events first in the list.

to.description: End of the time range to list events for, inclusive of the boundary. Defaults to now if omitted.

verbosity.description: How much rendering detail to include for events that produced a preview image. "none" omits image data entirely, keeping the response small; "thumbnail" includes a small preview link for each such event, which is useful when scanning a long history for the moment a render started looking wrong.

$ai_tools.name: list_clause_extraction_events_in_range

$ai_tools.description: Lists the organization's approved playbook clause templates, the source of truth the extraction pipeline scores extracted clauses against when computing a confidence value for standard versus nonstandard language. Templates are grouped by playbook; call get_playbook_by_key_and_org if you already know which playbook you care about and want its full template set in one call rather than the flattened list this tool returns across every playbook.

limit.description: Maximum number of playbook templates to return across the organization's playbooks.

organizationId.description: The organization whose playbook templates to list.

$ai_tools.name: list_organization_playbook_templates

$ai_tools.description: Searches the full text of every document attached to an organization's matters, such as base agreements, amendments, and exhibits, and returns the matching documents along with their matter and extraction status. Unlike search_clause_library, which searches curated playbook language, this searches the raw uploaded contract text, so it is the right tool when you need to find where a specific phrase actually appears in a customer's paperwork rather than in the organization's approved templates. Results are paginated with limit and offset since a broad query across a large workspace can match hundreds of documents.

limit.description: Maximum number of documents to return per page of results.

offset.description: Number of matching documents to skip before returning results, for paging through a large result set.

organizationId.description: The organization whose clause library to search.

query.description: Free-text query matched against document titles and their extracted text content, ranked by relevance.

$ai_tools.name: search_matter_documents_fulltext

$ai_tools.description: Fetches a single playbook by its key, including every approved clause template it contains and the fallback language used when an extracted clause matches no existing template closely enough. Playbook keys are stable across edits, so this is safe to cache for the duration of a debugging session rather than re-fetching on every call. Use list_organization_playbook_templates first if you do not already know which playbook key covers the clause category you are investigating.

organizationId.description: The organization that owns this playbook.

$ai_tools.name: get_playbook_by_key_and_org

$ai_tools.description: Returns a summary of an organization's ClauseIQ usage: active matters, documents processed in the last billing period, and the current average extraction confidence across clause categories. Useful as a quick, single-call sanity check for whether a fix improved things at the workspace level as a whole, before drilling into individual matters or extraction events to confirm exactly why the average moved.

organizationId.description: The organization to summarize, required for every call.

$ai_tools.name: get_organization_usage_and_confidence_summary

$ai_tools.description: Answers a free-text question against a single playbook's approved language, useful for checking whether a specific fallback position actually exists in the playbook before assuming the extraction pipeline invented language that was never approved by legal. Answers are grounded strictly in the playbook's own text and will say so plainly when nothing in the playbook addresses the question asked, rather than guessing at an answer.

playbookKey.description: The playbook to ask the question against.

organizationId.description: The organization that owns this playbook.

question.description: The question to answer against the playbook.

$ai_tools.name: ask_playbook_fallback_question

$ai_tools.description: Returns the active clause-extraction configuration for an organization and environment: the confidence thresholds that trigger a review flag per clause category, which playbook is bound as the default fallback, and the render settings used for diff previews. Compare staging against production when a regression only reproduces in one environment, since thresholds are sometimes tuned separately while a fix is being validated before it is promoted, and a threshold loosened in staging to unblock testing can easily be forgotten and left out of sync with production for weeks afterward, quietly masking the exact regression you are trying to reproduce. The optional matterId narrows the response to any matter-level overrides layered on top of the organization defaults, which matters most for a large customer who negotiated a bespoke threshold for one particularly sensitive matter; without it, the response only reflects the organization defaults, and a matter-level override is invisible, which can make a confidence drop look like a pipeline bug when it is actually working exactly as configured for that customer's matter alone.

organizationId.description: The organization whose configuration to read. Required in every environment.

$ai_tools.name: get_extraction_configuration

$ai_tools.description:
Lists confidence-threshold alerts that have fired for an organization, each
covering one clause category on one matter crossing below its configured
threshold. An alert stays active until either the confidence recovers on a
later extraction pass or a reviewer manually clears it, so a growing list
here alongside a shrinking list from list_matters_pending_confidence_review
usually means new matters are being affected faster than existing ones are
recovering, which is the pattern worth chasing down before declaring a fix
complete. Pair this with list_clause_extraction_events_in_range when you
need to see exactly which extraction run caused a given alert to fire,
rather than only that it fired.

This always returns active alerts only; a cleared alert drops off the list
entirely rather than being marked cleared in place, so a workspace that has
been running for a while does not accumulate a long tail of stale entries
here. Use responseDetail to control how much evidence comes back per
alert: "summary" is enough for a first pass across many matters, while
"full" is worth the extra payload once you have narrowed down to a
handful of alerts you actually need to investigate, since it also
includes the confidence history leading up to the point the alert fired.

detail.description: How much detail to include per alert. "summary" keeps the response small and is enough for a first pass across many matters; "full" includes the evidence and confidence history behind each alert, which is worth the extra payload once you have narrowed down to a handful of alerts.

clauseCategory.description: Restrict to alerts for this clause category, such as indemnification or termination, rather than every category the alert list would otherwise cover across the organization.

organizationId.description: The organization to list confidence alerts for.

matterId.description: Restrict to alerts for this matter only, instead of every matter in the organization, which is the fastest way to check one specific customer's status.

$ai_tools.name: list_confidence_alerts
